summary: ORBIT (Observation and Real-time Biometric Information Tracker) is an AI-powered health monitoring platform designed to help astronauts manage their physical well-being during extended space missions. It tracks five essential biometric indicators: heart rate, oxygen levels, respiration, hydration, and body temperature, providing real-time assessments and alerts for potential health hazards caused by radiation, isolation, distance, gravity, and environment. Beyond monitoring, ORBIT identifies possible health risks, recommends guided activities to regulate abnormal indicators, and features body-focused assessments for the head, chest, spine, and legs. Its integrated AI chatbot, powered by Gemini and NASA-based health information, provides accessible explanations and health guidance, enabling astronauts to better understand their conditions and make informed decisions. Ultimately, ORBIT transforms health monitoring into proactive self-care, supporting astronaut safety and well-being throughout humanity's exploration beyond Earth.
details:
What it does and how it works

The ORBIT (Observation and Real-time Biometric Information Tracker) Health Monitoring System is an advanced, data-driven web application built to monitor, simulate, and analyze spacesuit telemetry and astronaut vital signs in real-time. The platform centers around an interactive dashboard featuring a Heads-Up Display (HUD) and a 3D astronaut model to visually map incoming biometric data. Behind the scenes, a health risk engine continuously processes these physiological metrics against simulated NASA environmental hazards to maintain a constant read on crew status.

Benefits

ORBIT equips flight surgeons and mission controllers with instant, critical insights into the health of their crew. By automating the monitoring of environmental hazards, suit systems, and self-assessments, the platform significantly reduces the cognitive burden on operators. This streamlined approach enables faster diagnosis of physiological issues and allows for more effective workload distribution to mitigate health risks during active missions.

Intended Impact

With human spaceflight expanding toward the Moon and Mars, ORBIT is designed to be a scalable, responsive bedrock for future autonomous and predictive medical systems. The project seeks to guide mission planners and space agencies in determining the optimal timing and methods for medical interventions. Ultimately, it aims to minimize the extreme risks of extraterrestrial environments and pave the way for safer long-duration space exploration.

Tools, Coding Languages, and Software Used

  • Backend: Laravel (PHP) powers the core architecture, dataset management, and health risk engine.
  • Frontend: React (TypeScript) bundled with Vite delivers a fast, responsive user interface.
  • Real-Time Data: Laravel Reverb is implemented for WebSocket-based live telemetry broadcasting, ensuring immediate and resilient data delivery.

How the project is creative

ORBIT's creativity stems from translating dense, complex aerospace data into a highly visual and user-centric experience. Moving beyond traditional static tables, it leverages a real-time HUD and interactive 3D modeling for data visualization. Furthermore, it integrates a conversational AI-powered NASA Chatbot that acts as a co-pilot for operators, helping them interpret intricate biometrics, diagnose system alerts, and make swift, data-driven decisions.

Factors considered

A primary architectural consideration was system resilience and the absolute necessity of real-time data delivery, achieved through WebSockets and Reverb. The team also heavily factored in the unique environmental hazards and physical constraints of spaceflight, custom-building the risk engine and database to process specialized aerospace metrics such as NASA-defined hazards and spacesuit failures. Finally, user experience was prioritized to guarantee that the interface remains clear and intuitive for mission controllers operating under high-stress conditions.

Growing Investment in Space Health and Biomedical Innovation

The global space economy continues to attract substantial investment from governments, private enterprise, and research institutions, extending beyond spacecraft and satellite development into biomedical research and human spaceflight innovation. With the global space economy projected to reach $1.8 trillion by 2035, the expanding investment landscape reflects increasing opportunities for technologies that address the physiological challenges of space exploration. Furthermore, external research funding and commercial participation in space-based studies demonstrate that investment in the ecosystem is not limited to NASA alone. This creates a promising environment for innovative health-monitoring solutions that support physiological assessment, early identification driven health management for human spaceflight.

BUSINESS MODEL

ORBIT will be offered as a software platform that institutions can license annually. The platform will provide biometric monitoring, health-risk information, guided self-care recommendations, and AI-assisted health information.

Profitability

To determine whether ORBIT can become financially sustainable, we need to estimate the cost of developing, operating, and maintaining the platform.

Three-year financial projection

For a conservative scenario, let's assume ORBIT acquires one institutional client in Year 1, adds one in Year 2, and adds two more in Year 3.

Financial interpretation:

  • Year 1: ORBIT operates at a loss because initial development and implementation expenses are higher than its first contract revenue.
  • Year 2: Revenue increases as the platform gains another institutional client, although expenses remain higher than revenue.
  • Year 3: ORBIT achieves annual operating profitability, with an estimated operating profit of approximately $29,700.
  • The projected Year 3 operating margin is approximately 27.1%.

3. Sustainability

ORBIT's sustainability should not depend solely on acquiring new clients. It should establish recurring revenue and long-term institutional partnerships.

A. Recurring institutional subscriptions

Annual licensing provides predictable revenue that can finance regular software updates, cloud infrastructure, AI services, and technical support.

B. Continuous product development

A portion of revenue will be allocated to improving biometric monitoring, enhancing the AI chatbot, strengthening data security, and integrating additional compatible health-monitoring devices.

C. Research and institutional partnerships

ORBIT can pursue collaborations with space agencies, universities, aerospace companies, and health research institutions. These partnerships may provide opportunities for pilot testing, technical validation, and further development.

D. Scalable deployment

As ORBIT becomes more mature, it can be adapted for different mission environments and institutional requirements. Its software-based model allows expansion without necessarily developing an entirely new platform for every customer.

E. Grants and innovation funding

During its early development stage, ORBIT may also seek research grants, technology-development programs, and innovation funding. These can help finance testing and validation before the platform becomes commercially deployable.

Related Literature

The following studies and research provide the scientific foundation for ORBIT's development:

- In NASA (2024), "Wearable Tech for Space Station Research", researchers explored wearable monitoring devices used by astronauts to track heart activity, breathing patterns, sleep quality, and physical performance. Findings demonstrated the potential of wearable sensors for continuous health monitoring during space missions.

- In Auñón-Chancellor, et al. (2020), "Venous Thrombosis during Spaceflight", researchers documented a case of an astronaut who developed a blood clot in the internal jugular vein during an ISS mission without experiencing noticeable symptoms. The case highlighted the importance of health monitoring and early detection of potential medical complications in space.

- In Stenger, et al. (2019), "Assessment of Jugular Venous Blood Flow Stasis and Thrombosis During Spaceflight", researchers examined 11 ISS crew members and found that six experienced stagnant or reversed blood flow in the internal jugular vein, while one developed an obstructive blood clot. The findings demonstrated how microgravity can affect cardiovascular health.

- In NASA (2021), "Human Adaptation to Spaceflight", researchers examined the physiological effects of prolonged spaceflight, including fluid redistribution, reduced blood volume, bone density loss, and hydration challenges. The report emphasized the importance of maintaining proper hydration and monitoring physiological changes to preserve astronaut health.

- In Gupta and Ghosh (2025), "Advancements in Health Monitoring Technologies for Astronauts in Deep Space Missions: A Review", researchers reviewed developments in wearable sensors, physiological monitoring, and AI-driven health assessment for astronauts. The study highlighted the need for more autonomous and intelligent monitoring systems to support medical care during deep-space missions.
